reference.source: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Defined by a clinical triad of encephalopathy, branch retinal artery occlusions, and sensorineural hearing loss, though all three are often not present at onset
Predominantly affects young women and may be misdiagnosed as multiple sclerosis or migraine with aura
Encephalopathy can include headache, confusion, cognitive and behavioural change, and focal deficits
MRI characteristically shows central callosal lesions described as 'snowball' or 'icicle' lesions, differing from the peripheral callosal lesions of multiple sclerosis
Fluorescein angiography reveals branch retinal artery occlusions and arterial wall hyperfluorescence even in asymptomatic segments
Audiometry typically shows low- to mid-frequency sensorineural hearing loss from cochlear microinfarction
Early aggressive immunosuppression aims to limit permanent cognitive, visual, and auditory damage
reference.pathophysiology: Susac syndrome is an immune-mediated microangiopathy (endotheliopathy) affecting the small vessels (precapillary arterioles) of the brain, retina, and inner ear. Antiendothelial cell antibodies and cytotoxic lymphocyte-mediated injury to microvascular endothelium are implicated, producing microvascular occlusion and ischaemic damage in these three organs. Involvement of the corpus callosum microvasculature yields the characteristic central callosal MRI lesions, retinal arteriolar occlusion causes visual deficits, and cochlear microinfarction produces hearing loss and vertigo.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple sclerosis and acute disseminated encephalomyelitis
Antiphospholipid syndrome and other thrombotic microangiopathies
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain looking for central corpus callosum 'snowball' lesions and leptomeningeal enhancement
Fluorescein angiography to detect branch retinal artery occlusions and arterial wall hyperfluorescence
Audiometry to identify and monitor sensorineural hearing loss
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showing raised protein but usually without oligoclonal bands
Autoimmune and thrombophilia screen to exclude mimics
Serial ophthalmological review including retinal imaging
redFlags: Rapidly progressive encephalopathy with cognitive decline
Acute visual loss from retinal artery occlusion
New focal neurological deficits indicating ongoing microinfarction
reference.prognosis: The disease is often self-limiting over months to a few years but can leave permanent cognitive impairment, visual field loss, and hearing deficits; early and sustained immunosuppression improves outcomes, though relapses occur.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as multiple sclerosis and missing the distinguishing central callosal lesions
Not performing fluorescein angiography, thereby missing subclinical retinal artery occlusions
Overlooking the diagnosis when the full triad is not present at onset
Under-treating early disease and permitting irreversible organ damage
Attributing cognitive symptoms to a psychiatric cause
management: Institute prompt, aggressive immunosuppression with high-dose corticosteroids, usually combined with intravenous immunoglobulin, to halt the microvascular injury
Add steroid-sparing immunosuppression such as mycophenolate, azathioprine, rituximab or cyclophosphamide in severe or refractory encephalopathic disease
Escalate to pulse corticosteroids with intravenous immunoglobulin or cyclophosphamide during acute encephalopathic deterioration
Provide rehabilitation for cognitive deficits and hearing rehabilitation with hearing aids or cochlear implantation for sensorineural loss
Monitor disease activity with serial brain MRI, fluorescein angiography and audiometry, since subclinical relapse is common
Manage through a multidisciplinary team spanning neurology, ophthalmology and audiology or ENT
Continue prolonged immunosuppression and surveillance because relapses occur after apparent remission
